strengths: Proposes a new self-supervised learning strategy, Equivariant Splitting (ES), for inverse problems with a single incomplete forward operator, combining ideas from measurement splitting and equivariant imaging.

Introduces a useful definition of equivariance for reconstruction functions and shows that several common reconstruction architectures (artifact removal, unrolled networks, Reynolds averaging, MAP, MMSE) satisfy it under natural assumptions.

Provides theoretical results showing that the ES loss has the MMSE estimator as a global minimizer under a full-rank condition, and that with an equivariant reconstructor the ES loss reduces to the standard splitting loss, avoiding explicit transformation overhead.

Experiments on image inpainting, accelerated MRI, and compressive sensing show that ES consistently outperforms the equivariant imaging baseline and approaches supervised performance. The ablation study provides evidence for the benefit of using equivariant architectures with splitting losses.
The paper is generally well-written, well-organized, and clearly positions itself with respect to related work on measurement splitting and equivariant imaging.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: ES combines existing measurement splitting with existing equivariance assumptions, and Theorem 3 shows that with an equivariant architecture the proposed loss is equivalent to a standard splitting loss. This makes the core practical contribution feel closer to an architecture/design insight than a fundamentally new training objective.

The theoretical guarantees rely on strong assumptions that are difficult to verify in practice, such as full rank of Q_{A1} or ̄Q_A. The paper does not empirically verify these conditions on the considered problems. Additionally, the abstract and introduction suggest unbiased estimates of the supervised loss, but the analysis mainly establishes a weighted-risk minimizer rather than an unbiased supervised-loss estimator.

There are some technical gaps in the proofs. For example, the MMSE equivariance proof assumes p(A) is invariant although the theorem statement only assumes p(x) is invariant. The equivalence in Theorem 3 relies on the splitting distribution being invariant to the group action, which is not explicitly stated or discussed.

The experimental evaluation is limited in scope: only one unrolled architecture is used, the baselines are mainly EI, SURE/MC, and supervised/learning-free methods, and there is no comparison to other recent self-supervised inverse-problem methods. The datasets are relatively small or low-resolution (MNIST, 128x128 DIV2K crops, 320x320 single-coil FastMRI), and no code or reproducibility artifacts are provided.

Reported improvements over EI are meaningful but sometimes modest, and there is little hyperparameter sensitivity analysis or quantification of the claimed computational savings. Statistical significance of the reported gains is not assessed despite reporting standard deviations.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: self-supervised learning for inverse problems when only a single incomplete forward operator is available.
Combines measurement splitting and equivariance ideas in a principled way, with theoretical results attempting to connect ES to MMSE-optimal reconstruction.
Introduces a definition of equivariant reconstructors and shows several standard architectures/estimators satisfy it under an invariant signal prior.
Provides experiments on three imaging inverse problems (compressive sensing, inpainting, accelerated MRI) with several baselines and an ablation on equivariant architectures.
The paper is generally well organized and the motivation and method are clearly presented.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is not sound as written: Theorem 1's proof replaces the virtual signal x_g=T_g^{-1}x by x, so the stated minimizer f*(y1,A1)=E[x|y1,A1] appears inconsistent with the ES loss, which should target x_g for each virtual operator. The MMSE-optimality claim is therefore not rigorously established.

Theorem 2's proof for MAP/MMSE equivariance assumes p(A) is invariant and independent of x, but the paper's setting uses a fixed forward operator A; this mismatch weakens the claimed generality of the equivariant-reconstructor results.

There is an unresolved issue with the test-time procedure in eq. (12): averaging f(y1,A1) over randomly sampled transformations g without transforming back may produce an average of x_g rather than x, which is not justified for equivariant f.

The methodological novelty is incremental: the core idea is to combine existing splitting losses with existing equivariant architectures. If f is exactly equivariant, Theorem 3 shows ES reduces to ordinary splitting with A, so the new loss itself contributes little beyond architectural constraints.

The ablation undermines the central message: non-equivariant architectures trained with splitting perform close to equivariant ones (e.g., inpainting 27.20 vs 27.45 PSNR, MRI 28.18 vs 28.54), suggesting learned equivariance or other factors dominate and the proposed synergy is not the main driver.

Experimental evaluation is narrow: MNIST compressive sensing, 128x128 DIV2K inpainting with a single 30% mask, and fastMRI with a single mask. Despite claiming broad applicability, no sparse-view CT or other modalities are tested.

Baseline comparisons are limited to EI, SURE, MC, and simple inversion/IDFT. Stronger single-operator self-supervised baselines are missing, and the reported gains over EI are modest in several settings.
State-of-the-art and unbiasedness claims are overstated given the theoretical gaps, limited evaluation, and the fact that supervised baselines still consistently outperform the method.

Reproducibility and clarity issues: test-time averaging is unclear, EI and ES use different transformation groups, training requires up to 50 GPU hours per model with no code release mentioned, and some table entries are suspicious (e.g., supervised EQUIV equals PSNR in Table 2).

strengths: Introduces Equivariant Splitting (ES), a novel self-supervised loss that combines measurement splitting with invariance-based virtual operators, with theoretical guarantees of MMSE optimality under mild assumptions.
Provides a new definition of equivariance for reconstruction networks f(y,A) and proves that many common architectures (artifact-removal, unrolled networks, Reynolds averaging, MAP, MMSE) satisfy it.

Shows that for equivariant reconstructors the ES loss reduces to the standard splitting loss, eliminating the need for explicit transformation evaluations and reducing computational cost relative to equivariant imaging.

Employs strong theoretical analysis: Theorem 1 establishes MMSE-optimality, Corollary 1 clarifies when transformations allow learning beyond the nullspace, and Theorem 3 gives an efficient implementation for equivariant architectures.

Empirical results on compressive sensing, image inpainting, and accelerated MRI demonstrate that ES outperforms EI and SURE and approaches supervised performance, with an ablation confirming the synergy between splitting losses and equivariant architectures.
Good reproducibility: uses public datasets (MNIST, DIV2K, fastMRI) and the DeepInverse library, and provides detailed experimental settings and error bars.
weaknesses: Evaluation is somewhat limited: compressive sensing uses MNIST, inpainting uses a single DIV2K setting, and MRI covers one anatomy. Comparisons are mainly against EI, SURE, and simple baselines, omitting several recent single-operator self-supervised methods.

The equivalence in Theorem 3 may rely on the splitting distribution being independent of the transformation g; if the conditional splitting distribution depends on g, the averaged ES loss could differ from the standard splitting loss in a way that is not fully addressed.
The claimed efficiency advantage over equivariant imaging is not quantified with runtime, memory, or number-of-evaluations tables, despite being a central motivation.
No code repository is provided for exact reproducibility, and hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., R2R α, training length, weighting) is not systematically studied.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art' performance is stronger than the evidence: only a few self-supervised baselines are compared, and no specialized MRI or inpainting self-supervised methods are evaluated.

strengths: Combines measurement splitting and equivariant imaging for single-operator inverse problems, with theoretical results linking equivariant reconstructors to MMSE optimality.
Introduces a new definition of equivariant reconstructor and sufficient conditions for common architectures such as artifact-removal, unrolled, Reynolds-averaged, MAP, and MMSE networks.

Theorem 3 shows a useful computational simplification: for equivariant reconstructors, the proposed equivariant splitting loss reduces to the standard splitting loss, avoiding explicit transformation evaluations.

Provides experiments on multiple modalities (compressive sensing, inpainting, accelerated MRI, sparse-view CT), including real MRI measurements and noisy settings, generally outperforming the EI baseline and approaching supervised performance.
Includes reproducibility details, algorithm pseudocode, training durations, and an ablation study on the effect of equivariant architectures.
weaknesses: Novelty and positioning are weakened because single-operator measurement splitting has already been explored, notably in SSDU (Yaman et al., 2020) for MRI; the paper does not compare against or adequately discuss this line of work, undermining the claim of being the first to extend splitting to the single-operator setting.

The actual training algorithm (Algorithm 1) uses the standard splitting loss, not the proposed equivariant splitting loss with explicit transformations; since Theorem 3 shows ES reduces to splitting for equivariant networks, the new loss is not used in practice and the core contribution becomes mainly an architecture constraint.

The theoretical guarantees rely on strong, unverified conditions such as full rank of Q_{A1} or \bar{Q}_A and noiseless measurements; these conditions are not empirically checked, and the noisy case is only informally argued via R2R without a rigorous proof.

The evaluation lacks important baselines, including SSDU, Noise2Inverse for CT, equivariant plug-and-play methods (Terris et al., 2024), and recent self-supervised MRI reconstruction methods, making the empirical claims less convincing.

Improvements over the EI baseline are sometimes modest (e.g., MRI PSNR +0.66, inpainting +1.56) and lack statistical significance testing; the ablation is limited to inpainting and MRI and does not cover compressive sensing or CT.

Presentation and notation have issues: inconsistent use of f(y,A) vs. f(A,x), messy tables, overclaiming language, and a proof of Theorem 2 (point 5) that invokes invariance of p(A) despite A being fixed, even if the conclusion may remain true.
Reproducibility is incomplete: despite a statement about sharing implementation, no code link is provided, and some hyperparameters and training details are missing or only partially specified.

strengths: Combines measurement splitting and equivariant imaging into a single self-supervised framework for inverse problems with a single incomplete forward operator.
Introduces a formal definition of equivariant reconstructors and shows that several common architectures (artifact-removal, unrolled, Reynolds averaging, MAP, MMSE) satisfy it.
Experiments cover multiple imaging modalities (inpainting, compressive sensing, accelerated MRI, sparse-view CT) with results competitive against supervised and EI baselines.
Includes an ablation study on the effect of equivariant architectures and reports training durations.
Reproducibility statement and use of standard datasets/libraries are positive.
weaknesses: A central theoretical claim is flawed: Theorem 3 shows that for equivariant reconstructors the proposed ES loss reduces exactly to the standard splitting loss. Thus the intended method does not actually exploit transformations during training; it is just measurement splitting combined with an equivariant architecture. The optimality proof in Theorem 1 is for the unrestricted ES loss over all functions, not for split loss over equivariant functions, so the MMSE guarantee does not apply to the method as implemented.

The equivariant class is too restrictive to guarantee MMSE recovery: split loss only supervises observed measurements, and many equivariant functions can achieve the same split loss while differing arbitrarily on missing components. This undermines the claim that the method learns beyond the nullspace of A in the single-operator setting.

Theorem 1 states full rank of Q_{A1} for 'some split', but the expected loss averages over all splits. The proof requires full rank for every split in the support; otherwise the minimizer can differ from MMSE for splits where Q is rank-deficient. The condition is insufficient as stated.

Proposition 1 involves inaccessible weighting matrices Q and uses them to define a corrected estimator, but practical inference uses a simple unweighted average over splits. This creates a substantial theory-practice gap and means the theoretical MMSE combination is not actually evaluated.

Novelty is limited: the paper combines two known ideas (measurement splitting and equivariant networks) and, due to Theorem 3, the proposed loss collapses to standard splitting for the architectures used. The paper also claims 'first to leverage equivariant networks to learn from incomplete data alone' but prior work used equivariant denoising blocks in unrolled inverse-problem architectures.

The EQUIV metric is not a reconstruction quality measure and can be trivially inflated by constant or overly smooth outputs (e.g., constant outputs give infinite EQUIV). Presenting it alongside PSNR/SSIM as a performance metric is misleading.

Baseline comparisons are potentially unfair or incomplete. In Table 6, non-equivariant EI outperforms the equivariant EI used in the main paper (e.g., inpainting 26.33 vs 25.89 PSNR), suggesting the main EI baseline may be weakened. No comparisons are made to other single-operator self-supervised methods (e.g., SSDU, Noise2Self-style approaches, etc.).

Computational cost is understated. Although ES uses one forward pass per iteration, it requires vastly more training epochs than supervised learning (e.g., MRI: 13,800 epochs vs 200 for supervised, ~92 hours vs ~1.6 hours according to Table 10). The practical efficiency advantage over supervised methods is therefore not demonstrated.

The observed benefit of explicit equivariance is small: in the ablation, equivariant architectures improve PSNR by only ~0.25 dB (inpainting) and ~0.36 dB (MRI) over non-equivariant architectures. This weakens the claimed synergy and the importance of the proposed theory.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence: the paper asserts state-of-the-art performance and MMSE-optimal recovery, but the theoretical conditions are not met by the implemented method and the experimental gains over strong baselines are modest or confounded by training length.
Writing and presentation issues: some references are malformed, tables/figures are difficult to parse, and the manuscript lacks a code link despite the reproducibility statement.

strengths: Introduces Equivariant Splitting (ES), a novel self-supervised loss for the challenging single incomplete forward operator setting by combining measurement splitting with equivariance and virtual operators {A T_g}.

Provides a new definition of equivariant reconstructors f(y, A T_g) = T_g^{-1} f(y, A) and characterizes several classical reconstruction families (artifact removal, unrolled networks, Reynolds averaging, MAP, MMSE) as satisfying this property under suitable assumptions.

Theoretical analysis is a strength: Theorem 1 shows that under a full-rank condition on Q_{A1} the ES minimizer equals the MMSE estimator, Theorem 3 shows that for equivariant reconstructors ES reduces to standard splitting, and Corollary 1 gives a useful necessary condition on non-equivariant forward operators.

Broad empirical evaluation across image inpainting, compressive sensing, accelerated MRI with synthetic and real measurements, and sparse-view CT. ES consistently outperforms the equivariant imaging baseline and remains close to the supervised upper bound.

Computational motivation is clear: ES requires only one network pass per training iteration, unlike equivariant imaging which typically needs two to three passes, leading to faster epochs and a practical advantage.
The appendix contains detailed proofs, architecture descriptions, transformation-choice guidelines, and additional experiments, which supports reproducibility and technical understanding.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee relies on the full-rank condition for Q_{A1} or \bar Q_A, but this condition is not empirically verified in the main experiments. In practice the method uses an unweighted average over random splits, which is not exactly the theoretically optimal weighted combination from Proposition 1, so there remains a gap between theory and practical inference.

The noisy measurement extension is not fully rigorous. The R2R loss is borrowed from denoising and applied to general A1 inside a reconstruction network; it is not clearly proven to remain an unbiased estimator of the clean measurement-consistency term for arbitrary incomplete operators, so the noisy-case MMSE claim is less supported than the noiseless case.

The novelty is somewhat incremental: the method essentially combines existing measurement splitting with equivariant architectures/equivariant imaging, using virtual operators A T_g to obtain implicit multi-operator diversity. The main theorem can be seen as a natural extension of known splitting arguments.

Some theoretical details are imprecise: Theorem 2's MMSE/MAP proofs contain unnecessary or incorrect invariance assumptions on p(A) and do not address non-uniqueness of MAP solutions; several conditional-expectation steps in Theorem 1 are notationally opaque and would benefit from clarification.

Evaluation has gaps: no multiple-training-run significance tests, limited baseline set for self-supervised MRI/CT, and supervised baselines are trained for far fewer epochs than ES/EI in some settings, which may not give a fully fair convergence comparison. The claim of "state-of-the-art" performance is therefore somewhat stronger than the evidence presented.

The EQUIV metric sometimes equals PSNR exactly in the reported tables (e.g., inpainting, CT), which is unexplained and possibly indicates normalization or implementation subtleties. A clearer definition and sanity check of this metric would strengthen the empirical claims.
Reproducibility is only partially supported: the paper states that code is shared, but no explicit repository or link is provided in the manuscript.
